findings.question: For claude-review.yml (automation/agent mode, prompt is set, fetch-depth 0): what repository content is placed in the model context? Does the action send whole files or only what the model requests through tools?
findings.answer:
The workflow runs in agent mode. Mode detection returns "agent" for a pull_request event whose action is opened, synchronize or ready_for_review whenever the prompt input is set (src/modes/detector.ts:64-76), and claude-review.yml sets prompt at line 30.

In agent mode the action prefetches nothing from GitHub. prepareAgentMode writes the prompt file from context.inputs.prompt alone (src/modes/agent/index.ts:72-80), and generatePrompt returns the raw prompt for agent mode before any GitHub data is formatted (src/create-prompt/index.ts:455-457). There is no call to fetchGitHubData in agent mode.

So the first provider call carries only: the literal prompt text from claude-review.yml lines 30 to 34 (which contains the pull request number, the path docs/superpowers/specs/2026-08-26-heleos-spark-foundation-design.md, and the names CLAUDE.md and ROADMAP.md), the claude_code system prompt preset (base-action/src/parse-sdk-options.ts:248-254), and the tool schemas, including the github_inline_comment MCP server that is installed because the allowlist names mcp__github_inline_comment__ (src/mcp/install-mcp-server.ts:80-82).

Everything else is pull, not push. The action sends no file bodies and no diff text of its own. Repository content enters the context only as tool results, and each tool result is then included in the next provider call. The reachable set is large: the action's own documentation states that by default Claude has access to "File operations (reading, committing, editing files, read-only git commands)" and that --allowedTools adds tools rather than replacing that base (docs/configuration.md:225-231, 244). On top of that base the workflow allows Bash(git diff *), Bash(git log *), Bash(gh pr comment:*), and three test or check commands (claude-review.yml line 35). Because actions/checkout runs with fetch-depth 0 (line 25), the entire git history is on the runner, so git log and git diff can reach any commit and any historical file version, not only the pull request range.

Concretely, for a review run the content that reaches Anthropic is: the pull request diff as produced by git diff (full text of added and removed lines), plus the files the model chooses to read. Because the prompt names them explicitly, CLAUDE.md (7120 bytes), ROADMAP.md (65363 bytes) and the spec (23616 bytes) are close to certain to be read in full, about 96 KB of governed prose per run before the diff is counted.
findings.unverifiable: I could not verify from the action's source which built-in tools the Claude Code CLI auto-allows in headless agent mode with no --permission-mode flag; the claim that file reading is available by default rests on the action's own docs/configuration.md:225-227, not on code I read. I also could not confirm whether the permission pattern form Bash(git diff *) used in claude-review.yml line 35, which is not the documented Bash(cmd:*) prefix form, actually matches git diff invocations. If it does not match, git diff falls through to ask and is denied in headless mode, and the review would run on read tool output alone.

findings.question: For claude.yml (tag mode, no prompt, triggered by an @claude mention): what repository content is placed in the model context?
findings.answer:
The workflow runs in tag mode. With no prompt input, an issue_comment, pull_request_review_comment or pull_request_review event that contains the trigger phrase resolves to tag mode (src/modes/detector.ts:34-61), and claude.yml sets no prompt.

Unlike agent mode, tag mode prefetches GitHub data before the first provider call. prepareTagMode calls fetchGitHubData (src/modes/tag/index.ts:52-63), which issues PR_QUERY or ISSUE_QUERY, and createPrompt then formats the result into the prompt file (src/modes/tag/index.ts:104-110).

What is in that first call, by field:

| Item | Source |
|---|---|
| Title, author login, head and base branch, state, additions, deletions, total commit count, changed file count | src/github/data/formatter.ts:18-25 |
| Full pull request or issue body text | src/github/data/formatter.ts:35-48, src/create-prompt/index.ts:640-652 |
| Up to 100 comment bodies with author and timestamp | src/github/api/queries/github.ts:54-67, formatter.ts:50-70 |
| Up to 100 reviews with their bodies, and each review's inline comments with file path and line number | queries/github.ts:68-97, formatter.ts:72-126 |
| Changed file list as path, change type, and plus or minus line counts, with a git blob SHA per file | formatter.ts:128-146, fetcher.ts:341-370 |
| The triggering comment body verbatim | src/create-prompt/index.ts:684-693 |
| Repository name, event type, trigger username and display name, trigger phrase, tracking comment id | src/create-prompt/index.ts:674-683 |
| Images referenced in comments, downloaded to disk and offered to the Read tool | fetcher.ts:476, src/github/utils/image-downloader.ts:178-215, create-prompt/index.ts:632-637 |

No file contents and no patch text are prefetched. The changed file list is metadata only: path, change type, counts and blob SHA, never the bytes.

As in agent mode, file content arrives only through tools, but tag mode grants a wider set explicitly: Glob, Grep, LS, Read, the comment and CI MCP tools, and git add, commit, push and rm (src/modes/tag/index.ts:123-150), plus this workflow's own Bash allowlist for unittest, node --check and tools/ci/checks.py (claude.yml line 45). The generated instructions tell the model to read the repository's CLAUDE.md (create-prompt/index.ts:739 and 825) and, for pull requests, to run git diff origin/BASE...HEAD (create-prompt/index.ts:727 and 822). So the whole checkout is readable and any part of it can be sent. Because claude.yml checks out with fetch-depth 1 (line 40), the history available to git log and git diff is far narrower than in the review workflow.

One difference that matters for egress volume: tag mode can be fired from an issue as well as a pull request, and the job is an implementation job with contents: write, so a run can read broadly, edit, commit and push to a branch.
findings.unverifiable: Whether the model actually runs git diff in a claude.yml run cannot be established from source, only that the prompt instructs it to and that git is on the runner; the exact quantity of file content sent per run is therefore run dependent and not predictable from configuration.

findings.question: Does either workflow, as configured here, transmit anything that spec section 5 would class as SECRET? Does the action redact secrets from what it sends?
findings.answer:
Nothing SECRET is placed in the prompt by construction, but three separate facts qualify that answer, and two of them are real exposure paths.

First, CLAUDE_CODE_OAUTH_TOKEN is itself SECRET-class material under the section 5 table (API keys, tokens, credentials) and it is transmitted to Anthropic on every request, because it is the credential for that provider. Section 5's own rule is that SECRET is never placed in prompts, datasets, notebooks, logs or the repository. It is not placed in any of those. It is held in GitHub Actions secrets and sent as authentication. That is the ordinary meaning of interactive credential use, but a decision record should say so rather than leave it implied.

Second, both tokens sit in the environment of the process that runs the model loop and are not scrubbed. run.ts sets process.env.GITHUB_TOKEN and process.env.GH_TOKEN from the GitHub App or workflow token (src/entrypoints/run.ts:174-176). parse-sdk-options then copies the whole process environment into the SDK subprocess env, deleting only ACTIONS_ID_TOKEN_REQUEST_URL and ACTIONS_ID_TOKEN_REQUEST_TOKEN (base-action/src/parse-sdk-options.ts:224-236). CLAUDE_CODE_OAUTH_TOKEN is in that copy. The action's environment scrubber is not active: CLAUDE_CODE_SUBPROCESS_ENV_SCRUB is set only when allowed_non_write_users is non-empty (action.yml:265), and neither workflow sets that input. Both workflows' Bash allowlists exclude env and printenv, and tag mode's own source notes that in the headless SDK anything that falls through to ask is denied (src/modes/tag/index.ts:173-174), so there is no allowed command that dumps the environment. The material is reachable but not reachable by an allowed tool.

Third, and this is the concrete one: because ALLOWED_NON_WRITE_USERS is empty, configureGitAuth rewrites the origin remote to https://x-access-token:TOKEN@github.com/owner/repo.git (src/github/operations/git-config.ts:75-81), which writes a live GitHub token in cleartext into .git/config inside the checkout. That function runs in both modes (src/modes/agent/index.ts:51-64 and src/modes/tag/index.ts:88-101), because neither workflow sets ssh_signing_key or use_commit_signing. File reading is available by default (docs/configuration.md:225-227) and is granted explicitly in tag mode (src/modes/tag/index.ts:123-133). A single Read of .git/config would therefore put a live GitHub installation token into the model context and send it to Anthropic. The model has no reason to read that file, so this is a possible transmission, not a certain one, but nothing in the configuration prevents it.

On redaction: the action's redaction is narrow and does not cover this. sanitizeContent applies redactGitHubTokens (src/github/utils/sanitizer.ts:54-63 and 65-97), but only to GitHub-sourced text, that is titles, bodies, comments and review comments, and only for the literal patterns ghp_, gho_, ghs_, ghr_ and github_pat_. It is never applied to file contents, Bash output, or any tool result. There is no redaction of Anthropic keys or OAuth tokens anywhere in the action. The show_full_output warning in docs/security.md:136-149 is about what appears in Actions logs, not about what is sent to the provider.

The repository itself holds no secret files today: 49 tracked files, no .env, no credential fixtures.
findings.unverifiable: Whether the Read tool in headless agent mode can read a dotfile path such as .git/config without a permission prompt, and whether the CLI applies any of its own secret redaction to tool results before sending them, cannot be settled from the action's source; both live in the CLI binary I could not inspect. The .git/config exposure should be treated as plausible and worth a mitigation rather than as a demonstrated transmission.

findings.question: Is the volume bounded, and by what? Does the run make a fixed number of provider calls or an open-ended agentic loop?
findings.answer:
It is an open-ended agentic loop, not a fixed number of calls, and neither workflow sets the one control that would bound it.

The turn cap is optional and unset. maxTurns is passed to the SDK only if an options value exists (base-action/src/parse-sdk-options.ts:260), the action exposes no max_turns input at all (the action.yml input list runs trigger_phrase through bot_name and contains none), and the documented way to set one is claude_args with --max-turns (docs/configuration.md:216-221). Neither claude-review.yml line 35 nor claude.yml line 45 passes it. The loop runs until the model stops, iterating over SDK messages with no counter (base-action/src/run-claude-sdk.ts:161-172).

What does bound a run:

| Bound | Value here |
|---|---|
| GitHub job timeout | 30 minutes for claude-review, 60 minutes for claude |
| Tool allowlist | Only the listed Bash commands, the MCP tools, and the default file-reading tools |
| Prefetched GitHub data, tag mode only | GraphQL caps of 100 commits, 100 files, 100 comments, 100 reviews, and 100 comments per review |
| Readable corpus | The whole checkout: 49 tracked files, about 1.43 MB, plus full git history under claude-review's fetch-depth 0 |

So the prefetched half is hard-bounded and small. The tool-driven half is bounded only by the wall clock and by what is on disk. A worst case for a single claude-review run is the entire tracked repository plus historical revisions, resent in growing context on each successive turn, since each tool result is carried forward.

One further consequence for record keeping: the action does write a full transcript of every message and tool result to RUNNER_TEMP/claude-execution-output.json and exposes it as the execution_file output (base-action/src/run-claude-sdk.ts:19 and 184, src/entrypoints/run.ts:286-288). That file is the only artifact that could tell you after the fact what a run actually sent. Neither workflow uploads it, so today it is discarded with the runner.
sources: command: git ls-files -z | xargs -0 wc -c | tail -1 -> 1430363 total
findings.unverifiable: Token volume per run cannot be predicted; it depends on how many files the model reads and how many turns it takes. No usage cap other than the job timeout exists in either workflow.

findings.question: Given spec section 5's four classes and the actual content of this repository, what data class does the transmitted content fall in, and would that change at Phase 3 or 4?
findings.answer:
Today the transmitted content is INTERNAL.

Working through the four class definitions at spec lines 95 to 98:

| Class | Fits? | Why |
|---|---|---|
| PUBLIC | No | The definition is public standards pages, public manufacturer literature, and licensed public datasets. The repository is private and none of its documents are published |
| INTERNAL | Yes | The definition is company rules, internal benchmarks, and non-project estimating methods. CLAUDE.md is literally the company's operating rules. The spec is the architecture authority. ROADMAP.md sets internal thresholds, gates and benchmark criteria. The CI configuration, tooling and run records are internal method |
| PROJECT_CONFIDENTIAL | Not today | The definition is bid drawings, specifications, addenda, quotes and evidence crops. The repository holds 49 files and none of them are any of those |
| SECRET | Not by construction | No credential file is tracked. See the separate finding on the token that the action writes into .git/config on the runner |

The governing consequence is that INTERNAL's default external rule in the same table is "Local by default; provider access requires an explicit approved policy." That is exactly the gate. The workflows are not forbidden outright by section 5, and CLAUDE.md's prohibition on sending INTERNAL material externally is stated as holding until a policy permits it. Decision 12 is that policy. Section 5's seven-field record requirement applies to every submission, and the action produces no such record on its own.

The classification would change at Phase 3 and Phase 4, and the decision must be written to survive that.

The mechanism is simple: the action reads whatever is present in the checkout at the commit being reviewed, with no path filter, no allowlist of readable directories and no data-class awareness. .gitignore today has three lines, __pycache__/, *.pyc and .venv/, so it excludes nothing project related, and untracked files in the working tree are readable too. Phase 3 introduces sheet detections, schedule rows and reconciliation edges; Phase 4 introduces evidence objects, corrections and exports. The section 5 table names bid drawings, specifications, addenda, quotes and evidence crops as PROJECT_CONFIDENTIAL, and evidence crops are precisely a Phase 3 and Phase 4 artifact. The moment any such artifact, or a test fixture derived from one, lands in a path the checkout contains, an @claude run or a review run can read it and send it, and a diff that touches it would carry it. PROJECT_CONFIDENTIAL's rule is stricter than INTERNAL's: not an approved policy but "project- and provider-specific approval."

ROADMAP.md already carries the intent, in the Phase 3 exit condition that no run touching PROJECT_CONFIDENTIAL content has session_kind: web (ROADMAP.md line 141). But that condition governs the project's own session records; it places no constraint on a GitHub Actions run of this action. So an approval written as "Anthropic is approved for this repository's content" would silently widen from INTERNAL to PROJECT_CONFIDENTIAL the first time a drawing artifact enters the tree, with no second decision and no signal that the class changed.
sources: <repo>/CLAUDE.md, Do not section, final bullet: "Send INTERNAL or PROJECT_CONFIDENTIAL material to any external service"
<repo>/ROADMAP.md line 141 (Phase 3 exit: no run touching PROJECT_CONFIDENTIAL content has session_kind: web) and lines 133-151 (Phase 3 and Phase 4 artifacts)
command: git ls-files | awk -F/ '{print $1}' | sort -u -> .agents .claude .codex .github .gitignore CLAUDE.md README.md ROADMAP.md docs tests tools
findings.unverifiable: Whether Phase 3 and Phase 4 artifacts will actually be committed to this repository, versus held only in the content-addressed vault outside the working tree, is not settled anywhere I could find. The spec describes the vault as a content-addressed filesystem store (line 67) but does not say it sits outside the git working tree, and .gitignore does not exclude it. The classification therefore has to assume the artifacts can appear in the checkout unless a later decision forbids it.

findings.question: Under a Claude subscription (the CLAUDE_CODE_OAUTH_TOKEN path), is customer content used to train Anthropic's generative models by default? What is the retention period for inputs and outputs? Is there a setting that changes it, and who controls it?
findings.answer:
The OAuth token path is the consumer path. The action's own setup guide at the pinned commit says the token is a subscription credential: "Or `CLAUDE_CODE_OAUTH_TOKEN` for OAuth token authentication (Pro and Max users can generate this by running `claude setup-token` locally)". Anthropic's Claude Code data usage page treats those plans as consumer and says explicitly that Claude Code sessions are in scope: "Consumer users (Free, Pro, and Max plans): We give you the choice to allow your data to be used to improve future Claude models. We will train new models using data from Free, Pro, and Max accounts when this setting is on (including when you use Claude Code from these accounts)."

Training is not off by default in the contract's own framing. The Consumer Terms of Service (effective October 8, 2025) state: "We may use Materials to provide, maintain, and improve the Services and to develop other products and services, including training our models, unless you opt out of training through your account settings. Even if you opt out, we will use Materials for model training when: (1) you provide Feedback to us regarding any Materials, or (2) your Materials are flagged for safety review to improve our ability to detect harmful content, enforce our policies, or advance our safety research." That is opt-out language: permission to train exists unless the account holder has turned the setting off. Anthropic's August 28, 2025 announcement adds that every consumer account had to make an affirmative selection: "After October 8, you'll need to make your selection on the model training setting in order to continue using Claude." So the honest statement for the owner is not "training is on by default" or "off by default", it is: whether this repository's diffs train Anthropic's models depends entirely on one toggle inside the personal Claude account whose token is pasted into the secret.

Retention follows the same toggle. Claude Code data usage page: "Consumer users (Free, Pro, and Max plans): Users who allow data use for model improvement: 5-year retention period to support model development and safety improvements. Users who don't allow data use for model improvement: 30-day retention period." The consumer retention article adds: "If you allow us to use your chats or coding sessions to improve Claude, we may retain your data in a de-identified format for up to 5 years in our model training pipelines." Exceptions on top of that: "We retain inputs and outputs for up to 2 years and trust and safety classification scores for up to 7 years if your chat or session is flagged by our automated trust and safety systems as violating our Usage Policy", and feedback submissions are retained "for 5 years".

Who controls the setting: the individual account holder, not the repository and not an organization admin. Claude Code data usage page: "Privacy settings can be changed at any time at claude.ai/settings/data-privacy-controls." The privacy centre article on changing the setting describes it as a per-account toggle under "Help Improve our AI models" in personal Privacy settings. Turning it off is not retroactive in full: "Your data will still be included in model training that has already started and in models that have already been trained."

curl https://docs.claude.com/en/docs/claude-code/data-usage (HTTP 200), sections "Data training policy" and "Data retention"
curl https://www.anthropic.com/legal/consumer-terms (HTTP 200), "Effective October 8, 2025", section "Our use of Materials"
findings.unverifiable: I could not observe the actual state of any specific account's model improvement toggle, and no published page states a factory default for an account created today beyond "you can select your preference in the signup process". The owner must read the toggle in the account that will issue the token.

findings.question: Under a Console API key (ANTHROPIC_API_KEY), are the answers different? State both, plainly, so the owner can compare.
findings.answer:
Yes, materially different, and the difference is contractual rather than a setting.

The API key path runs under the Commercial Terms of Service (effective June 17, 2025), which state in their opening scope: "They govern Customer's use of Anthropic API keys and any other Anthropic offerings that references these Terms". Section B says: "Anthropic may not train models on Customer Content from Services." The privacy centre commercial article says: "By default, we will not use your inputs or outputs from our commercial products (e.g. Claude for Work, Anthropic API, Claude Gov, etc.) to train our models." The Claude Code page says the same in Claude Code terms: "Commercial users: (Team and Enterprise plans, API, 3rd-party platforms, and Claude Gov) maintain existing policies: Anthropic does not train generative models using code or prompts sent to Claude Code under commercial terms, unless the customer has chosen to provide their data to us for model improvement (for example, the Developer Partner Program)." The August 2025 consumer announcement confirms the boundary from the other side: "These updates do not apply to services under our Commercial Terms, including: Claude for Work, which includes our Team and Enterprise plans; Our API, Amazon Bedrock, or Google Cloud's Vertex API; Claude Gov and Claude for Education."

Retention on the API is a flat 30 days: "For Anthropic API users, we automatically delete inputs and outputs on our backend within 30 days of receipt or generation, except: When you use a service with longer retention under your control (e.g. Files API); When you and we have agreed otherwise (e.g. zero data retention agreement); If we need to retain them for longer to enforce our Usage Policy (UP); In compliance with the law". The same flagged-content exception applies: up to 2 years for inputs and outputs, up to 7 years for classification scores.

Two further differences the owner should weigh. First, confidentiality: Commercial Terms section E.1 says "Customer Content is Customer's Confidential Information", and section E.2 limits sharing to "Recipient's employees, agents, and advisors that have a need to know such Confidential Information and who are bound to obligations of confidentiality". The Consumer Terms page contains the word "confidential" zero times, so the subscription path carries no equivalent confidentiality undertaking. Second, a data processing agreement exists only on the commercial side: Commercial Terms section C says "Data submitted through the Services will be processed in accordance with the Anthropic Data Processing Addendum (\"DPA\"), which is incorporated into these Terms by reference."

Comparison table:

| Question | CLAUDE_CODE_OAUTH_TOKEN (Pro or Max subscription) | ANTHROPIC_API_KEY (Console, Commercial Terms) |
|---|---|---|
| Governing terms | Consumer Terms of Service | Commercial Terms of Service plus DPA |
| Model training on repository content | Permitted unless the individual turns the setting off; two carve-outs remain (feedback, safety-flagged sessions) | Contractually prohibited: "Anthropic may not train models on Customer Content from Services" |
| Who controls that | The individual account holder, at claude.ai/settings/data-privacy-controls | Nobody has a toggle to turn training on; the exception is an explicit opt-in such as the Development Partner Program |
| Retention of inputs and outputs | 5 years if the setting is on, 30 days if off | 30 days, with listed exceptions |
| Retention if flagged for Usage Policy violation | Up to 2 years for content, up to 7 years for classification scores | Up to 2 years for content, up to 7 years for classification scores |
| Content treated as confidential information | No such clause in the Consumer Terms | Yes, Commercial Terms E.1 |
| Data processing addendum and sub-processor rights | None | Yes, DPA incorporated by reference |
| Zero data retention reachable | No, consumer plans are excluded | Yes, on request and subject to approval |

findings.question: What is the zero data retention option, if one exists, who qualifies, and how is it requested?
findings.answer:
Zero data retention (ZDR) exists, it is not self-serve, and it is unreachable from a Pro or Max subscription.

Definition, from the Claude Platform documentation: "Under a ZDR arrangement, Anthropic does not store customer prompts or responses at rest after the API response is returned." The privacy centre article puts the same thing with its carve-outs: "Some Claude Platform (Claude API) and Claude Code for Enterprise customers, subject to Anthropic's approval, may have arrangements under which Anthropic does not store their inputs or outputs except where needed to comply with law or combat misuse or harm. Under these arrangements, Anthropic still retains User Safety classifier results in order to enforce our Usage Policy."

Who qualifies. The same article: "Under these agreements, the only products to which zero data retention applies are eligible Anthropic APIs, Anthropic products that use your Commercial organization API key (including Claude Code accessed via the API), and Claude Code for Enterprise plans." The platform docs say ZDR explicitly does not cover "Claude consumer products: Claude Free, Pro, and Max plans, including when customers on those plans use Claude's web, desktop, or mobile apps or Claude Code." For Claude Code specifically: "ZDR applies when Claude Code is used with API keys from a Commercial organization (an organization under Anthropic's Commercial Terms of Service, as distinct from a consumer Claude account) or through Claude Enterprise with ZDR enabled."

How it is requested. "To request ZDR for your organization, contact the Anthropic sales team. ZDR is enabled per organization; each new organization requires ZDR to be enabled separately by your account team, and enablement does not automatically extend to other organizations under the same account." The Claude Code ZDR page adds: "ZDR is not included in the standard Claude for Enterprise plan and cannot be enabled from your admin settings. It is available to qualified accounts and requires separate enablement by Anthropic."

Limits the owner should note even under ZDR. Flagged content is still retained: "Even with ZDR enabled, Anthropic may retain data where required by law or to address Usage Policy violations. If a session is flagged for a policy violation, Anthropic may retain the associated inputs and outputs for up to 2 years, consistent with Anthropic's standard ZDR policy." Certain models are excluded: "Claude Fable 5.1, Claude Mythos 5.1, Claude Fable 5, and Claude Mythos 5: These models require 30-day data retention and are not available under ZDR unless expressly authorized by Anthropic."

curl https://docs.claude.com/en/docs/claude-code/zero-data-retention (HTTP 200), intro and sections "Data retention for policy violations", "Request ZDR"

findings.question: Is there any published commitment about human review of submitted content, and under what circumstances?
findings.answer:
Yes, there is a published commitment, and it is narrow rather than absolute.

The clearest statement is on the consumer side, which is the side the OAuth token would use. Anthropic's privacy centre states: "Limited Access: By default, Anthropic employees cannot access your conversations unless: You explicitly consent to share your data with us as a part of giving us feedback (learn more). Review is needed to enforce our Usage Policy. In such cases, your conversation data is protected through strict access controls, only designated members of our Trust & Safety team may access this data on a need-to-know basis as a part of their evaluation process."

The trigger for that review is automated. The Consumer Terms say Materials will be used for model training even after opting out when "your Materials are flagged for safety review to improve our ability to detect harmful content, enforce our policies, or advance our safety research", and the privacy policy says the same for inputs and outputs. Both retention articles state the consequence: "We retain inputs and outputs for up to 2 years and trust and safety classification scores for up to 7 years if your chat or session is flagged by our automated trust and safety systems as violating our Usage Policy."

On the commercial side the commitment is contractual rather than descriptive. Commercial Terms E.2: "Recipient may only share Discloser's Confidential Information to Recipient's employees, agents, and advisors that have a need to know such Confidential Information and who are bound to obligations of confidentiality at least as protective as those provided in these Terms." Read with E.1 ("Customer Content is Customer's Confidential Information"), that is a need-to-know limit on human access with contractual force behind it, which the Consumer Terms do not contain.

Two Claude Code specific paths send transcripts to humans, and both require an explicit action, so neither fires in an unattended GitHub Actions run. The documentation says of the session quality survey follow up: "Nothing is uploaded unless you explicitly select Yes", and of /feedback: "When you run the /feedback command, a copy of your conversation history including code is sent to Anthropic."

There is also a published statement that some models carry mandatory review: the commercial retention article says "for Covered Models, we require limited data retention and review as a part of our safety work", and the platform docs say "Conversation content (your prompts and Claude's outputs) is not retained by default; the exception is Covered Models, which require 30-day retention." Whichever credential is chosen, the model the workflows run should be pinned to one that is not a Covered Model if that mandatory retention and review is unacceptable.

findings.question: Where does processing happen, and is there any published sub-processor list relevant to code content?
findings.answer:
Processing is in the United States by default, with transfers elsewhere permitted, and a sub-processor list exists but is published on a page I could not read.

Location. The privacy policy states: "Anthropic is a global company, and when you access our Services, your personal data is transferred to our servers in the US, or to other countries outside the European Economic Area (\"EEA\") and the UK for the purposes outlined in Section 2 of this Privacy Policy, for example to provide you with the Service, or to train our models, or to conduct research. This may be a direct provision of your personal data to us, or a transfer that we or a third party make. You can find more details about the affiliates and third parties we transfer data to, including their locations, in our Trust Center."

Geographic control exists only on the API side. The Claude Platform data residency page describes two settings: "Inference geo: Controls where model inference runs, on a per-request basis. Set through the inference_geo API parameter or as a workspace default. Workspace geo: Controls where data is stored at rest and where endpoint processing (such as image transcoding and code execution) happens. Configured at the workspace level in the Claude Console." The default is not US-pinned: for inference_geo, "global" is documented as "Default. Inference may run in any available geography for optimal performance and availability", against "us" which "Inference runs only in US-based infrastructure." Support is limited to "Claude 4.6 and later models". There is no equivalent published control for a Pro or Max subscription.

Sub-processors. The DPA (effective February 24, 2025) makes the list contractual for the commercial path: section C.1, "Customer grants Anthropic general authorization to engage the Subprocessors listed in Schedule 4, and any additional Subprocessors in accordance with Section C.3."; section C.3 gives notice of new sub-processors and a fifteen day window to object; Schedule 4 says "Anthropic's list of subprocessors is available at https://www.anthropic.com/subprocessors." That URL redirects to https://trust.anthropic.com/subprocessors. Nothing equivalent applies to a consumer subscription, because the DPA is incorporated by the Commercial Terms only.

One published sub-processor fact does bear directly on code content, from the Claude Code documentation: transcripts submitted through /feedback are "encrypted in transit via TLS and stored in Google Cloud Storage", and error reports go "to a third-party error tracking service". Neither path is triggered by an unattended Actions run.

findings.question: Where should an egress record live so that it is durable and reviewable: committed under docs/runs/, a workflow artifact, a job summary, or something else?
findings.answer:
Recommendation: the run writes the record in three places at once, and none of them is a commit made by the workflow.

| Place | What it holds | Why |
|---|---|---|
| Job summary (`$GITHUB_STEP_SUMMARY`) | The seven fields rendered as a table | Sits next to the run that made the submission, so a reviewer opening the run sees the record without leaving the page |
| Workflow artifact `egress-<workflow>-<run_id>-<attempt>` holding `egress.jsonl` | One JSON line, machine readable | Downloadable, diffable, and the input to the roll-up |
| `docs/runs/egress/index.jsonl`, appended by a periodic roll-up pull request | Every line from every expired and unexpired run | The durable, committed, hash-checkable ledger the spec's word record implies |

Why the workflow must not commit the record itself. First, on `pull_request` the checked-out ref is `refs/pull/N/merge` and `GITHUB_SHA` is the merge commit (GitHub docs, events-that-trigger-workflows: for `pull_request`, GITHUB_SHA is the "Last merge commit on the GITHUB_REF branch"), which is not a branch that can be pushed. Second, branch protection on `main` is Decision 6 and roadmap task P0.6, and requires a pull request before merging, so a job push to `main` is designed to fail. Third, pushing to the pull request head branch would fire `pull_request: synchronize`, which is exactly what re-triggers `claude-review` (`.github/workflows/claude-review.yml:5-6`), giving an unbounded loop, and it would race the `claude` workflow, which already pushes to that same branch (`docs/policies/github-automation.md:12`). Fourth, `claude-review` declares `contents: read` (`claude-review.yml:13`), so it has no push credential at all, and giving it one to write a log would widen the workflow's authority for the sake of the log.

What it costs. The artifact and the run logs expire: GitHub retains Actions artifacts and logs for 90 days by default, configurable between 1 and 400 days for a private repository (docs.github.com managing-github-actions-settings-for-a-repository, "Configuring the retention period for GitHub Actions artifacts and logs in your repository"). So between roll-ups the ledger is only as durable as that retention window, and a record never rolled up before it expires is gone. The roll-up therefore needs a cadence shorter than the retention setting and a person or session to run it, which is a standing manual obligation the decision record must name. The second cost is that the committed ledger is written by a different actor than the run that egressed, so the committed line is a transcription rather than a first-party artifact; the run URL inside `result_ref` is what lets a reviewer go back to the original while it still exists.

findings.question: What exactly can be filled in automatically for each of the seven fields from inside a GitHub Actions run, and what cannot? In particular, what is hashed for source hashes?
findings.answer:
| Field | Automatic? | What it is filled from | What is not captured |
|---|---|---|---|
| provider | Yes, as a constant | The literal `anthropic` in the workflow step. It is not derivable from the environment: the same action reaches Anthropic, Bedrock, Vertex or Foundry depending on `use_bedrock` / `use_vertex` / `use_foundry` and `ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL` (action.yml at the pinned commit). Since this repository sets none of those, the constant is correct, and a check can assert those inputs are absent | The actual endpoint contacted at runtime |
| purpose | Yes, as a constant | A literal string per workflow. It restates what the workflow is for, not what the model chose to do | Nothing meaningful; it is a declaration by design |
| data class | Declared, never measured | A literal `INTERNAL` per workflow, validated against the four spec classes and against the classes the caller may send | Whether the checkout actually contains `PROJECT_CONFIDENTIAL` bytes. Classification is a human judgment about content; no script can assert it |
| source hashes | Partly, as an upper bound | See below | The exact subset the model read |
| policy decision | Yes | The repository-relative path of `docs/policies/egress.md` and of the Decision 12 record, plus the SHA-256 of each file as checked out, plus a rule id and an allow or refused outcome. Because the decision file is hashed at the commit that ran, a later edit of the decision does not silently re-authorize old submissions | Nothing |
| time | Yes | UTC timestamp at the moment the record is written | The time of each individual API call. One run makes many calls over up to 30 or 60 minutes (`claude-review.yml:11`, `claude.yml:25`). The single timestamp marks the end of the submission window; the run URL carries the start and end |
| result reference | Yes | Run URL with attempt, job name, `GITHUB_WORKFLOW_REF`, the pull request or issue URL, the action's `session_id` output and the step conclusion. `session_id` and `execution_file` are real action outputs (action.yml outputs block; `src/entrypoints/run.ts` calls `core.setOutput("session_id", ...)` and `core.setOutput("execution_file", ...)`) | The content of the exchange. `execution_file` is the full transcript in `RUNNER_TEMP`; the action's own input docs warn it "may contain secrets, API keys, or other sensitive information" (`show_full_output` description), so it must not be retained or embedded, and hashing something nobody keeps proves nothing later |

Source hashes, concretely. The action does not receive a bundle of files. In agent mode, which is what `claude-review.yml` uses because it passes `prompt:`, the prompt written to disk is exactly the workflow's `prompt` input, with a fallback of only `Repository: owner/repo` (`src/modes/agent/index.ts`, lines around 73 to 79 at the pinned commit). Everything else, including the diff, is fetched by the model's own tools during the run. In tag mode, which is what `claude.yml` uses because it passes no prompt, `fetchGitHubData` pulls the issue or pull request body, its comments, its reviews and its changed files, and the action itself computes `git hash-object` per changed file (`src/github/data/fetcher.ts`, `changedFilesWithSHA`), then `createPrompt` embeds that data.

So the honest hash is not "the files sent" but "the boundary of what the run made available", recorded as labelled entries:

| Label | Value | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `checkout-tree:sha1:` | `git rev-parse HEAD^{tree}` | Content hash of the entire tree on disk. Reproducible: the same tree hash means byte-identical content |
| `checkout-commit:sha1:` | `GITHUB_SHA` | For `pull_request` this is the merge commit that was reviewed; for `issue_comment` it is the default branch head |
| `event-payload:sha256:` | SHA-256 of the file at `GITHUB_EVENT_PATH` | The untrusted text that triggered the run: pull request or issue title, body, and the triggering comment |
| `prompt-source:sha256:` | SHA-256 of the workflow file itself | The literal prompt text lives in the workflow file, so hashing the file pins the instruction that was sent |

What this deliberately does not claim. It is an upper bound, not a manifest. The model may read all of it or none of it. Worse for `claude.yml`: the action holds a GitHub token, and tag mode fetches comments and reviews through the API at run time, after the event payload was written, so the event-payload hash does not cover every piece of text submitted. Both workflows also allow `Bash(git diff *)` and `Bash(git log *)` or equivalents (`claude-review.yml:35`), so history outside the checked-out tree is reachable in the `fetch-depth: 0` case. The correct sentence for the ledger and the policy is: these hashes identify what the run made available at the moment the record was written, and the submitted subset is not observable from inside the run.

findings.question: What is the smallest addition to the two workflows plus a Python helper in the house style that emits the seven-field record, without leaking the token or any secret?
findings.answer:
Two new files and three new steps per workflow. Both files were written and run before being proposed: `python3 -m unittest discover -s tests -p 'test_*.py'` returns 9 tests, OK, exit 0. Verified copies are at /proposal/tools/egress/record.py and /proposal/tests/test_egress_record.py. Nothing was written into the repository. Design choices that matter. 1. Two modes in one script. `check` runs BEFORE the action and fails the job when `docs/policies/egress.md` or the named Decision 12 record is missing from the checkout, or when the declared class is not one this caller may send. That makes the record a gate, not a log: with no decision record in the tree, the Claude step never runs. `write` runs after with `if: always()`. 2. The record is exactly the seven fields, in the key names the operating model already declares at line 733: `provider, purpose, data_class, source_hashes, policy_decision, time, result_ref`. `serialise` raises if the field tuple is anything else, and a test asserts it. 3. Secret safety is structural, not filtered. The script reads only an eight-name `ENV_ALLOWLIST` of `GITHUB_*` variables. `CLAUDE_CODE_OAUTH_TOKEN`, `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY` and `GITHUB_TOKEN` are simply never read. A test pollutes the environment with all three token shapes and asserts none appears in the serialised line. A token-shape scan over the serialised record is the second layer: a match refuses the write with exit 1 and writes nothing. No pull request text, issue text, comment text or model output is ever copied in; sources appear only as hashes. 4. A failed precondition in `write` mode records `policy_decision.outcome: "refused"` and `decision_sha256: "absent"` and still writes the line, then exits 1. A submission that already happened must never become a missing line. The helper, `tools/egress/record.py` (237 lines, standard library only, snake_case, no em or en dash): ```python """Record one external submission made by a GitHub Actions run (spec section 5). The seven fields of spec section 5 are the whole record: provider, purpose, data_class, source_hashes, policy_decision, time, result_ref. No text taken from a pull request, an issue, a comment, a model answer, or the process environment beyond ENV_ALLOWLIST is ever copied into it; sources are named by hash, never by content. Subcommands: check Runs before the external call. Fails the job when the policy file or the decision record named on the command line is missing from the checkout, or when the declared data class is not one this caller may send. write Runs after the external call. Appends one JSON line to --out and a rendered copy to --summary. Standard library only. Exit code 1 on any failure. In check mode a failure writes nothing and stops the job before the call. In write mode the call has already happened, so a failure is recorded as a refused decision and still written, then reported with exit code 1. """ import argparse import hashlib import json import os import re import subprocess import sys from datetime import datetime, timezone ROOT = os.path.dirname(os.path.dirname(os.path.dirname(os.path.abspath(__file__)))) FIELDS = ("provider", "purpose", "data_class", "source_hashes", "policy_decision", "time", "result_ref") DATA_CLASSES = ("PUBLIC", "INTERNAL", "PROJECT_CONFIDENTIAL", "SECRET") ENV_ALLOWLIST = ( "GITHUB_SERVER_URL", "GITHUB_REPOSITORY", "GITHUB_RUN_ID", "GITHUB_RUN_ATTEMPT", "GITHUB_JOB", "GITHUB_SHA", "GITHUB_EVENT_PATH", "GITHUB_WORKFLOW_REF", ) SECRET_PATTERNS = ( ("github token", re.compile(r"gh[pousr]_[A-Za-z0-9]{16,}")), ("github pat", re.compile(r"github_pat_[A-Za-z0-9_]{20,}")), ("anthropic key or oauth token", re.compile(r"sk-ant-[A-Za-z0-9_-]{16,}")), ("api key", re.compile(r"\bsk-[A-Za-z0-9]{20,}")), ("aws access key id", re.compile(r"\bAKIA[0-9A-Z]{16}\b")), ("private key block", re.compile(r"-----BEGIN [A-Z ]*PRIVATE KEY-----")), ) def read_env(env): """Only these variables are ever read. A secret in the environment cannot reach a record.""" return {name: env[name] for name in ENV_ALLOWLIST if env.get(name)} def utc_now(): return datetime.now(timezone.utc).strftime("%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ") def sha256_file(path): digest = hashlib.sha256() with open(path, "rb") as handle: for block in iter(lambda: handle.read(65536), b""): digest.update(block) return digest.hexdigest() def git_tree(root): """SHA-1 of the tree that was on disk: the upper bound of what the provider could be shown.""" result = subprocess.run( ["git", "rev-parse", "HEAD^{tree}"], cwd=root, capture_output=True, text=True, check=True ) return result.stdout.strip() def source_hashes(root, env, prompt_source=None): """Labelled hashes of what the run made available, not of what the provider chose to read.""" hashes = ["checkout-tree:sha1:" + git_tree(root)] if env.get("GITHUB_SHA"): hashes.append("checkout-commit:sha1:" + env["GITHUB_SHA"]) event = env.get("GITHUB_EVENT_PATH") if event and os.path.exists(event): hashes.append("event-payload:sha256:" + sha256_file(event)) if prompt_source: hashes.append("prompt-source:sha256:" + sha256_file(os.path.join(root, prompt_source))) return hashes def sha256_or_absent(root, relative): """A missing file is recorded as absent rather than crashing, so no submission goes unrecorded.""" try: return sha256_file(os.path.join(root, relative)) except OSError: return "absent" def policy_decision(root, policy, decision, rule, outcome="allow"): return { "outcome": outcome, "rule": rule, "policy": policy, "policy_sha256": sha256_or_absent(root, policy), "decision": decision, "decision_sha256": sha256_or_absent(root, decision), } def result_ref(env, session_id=None, conclusion=None, entity_url=None): server = env.get("GITHUB_SERVER_URL", "") repository = env.get("GITHUB_REPOSITORY", "") run_id = env.get("GITHUB_RUN_ID", "") attempt = env.get("GITHUB_RUN_ATTEMPT", "1") reference = { "run_url": f"{server}/{repository}/actions/runs/{run_id}/attempts/{attempt}", "job": env.get("GITHUB_JOB", ""), "workflow_ref": env.get("GITHUB_WORKFLOW_REF", ""), } if entity_url: reference["entity_url"] = entity_url reference["provider_session_id"] = session_id or "not reported" reference["conclusion"] = conclusion or "not reported" return reference def check_preconditions(root, policy, decision, data_class, allowed_classes): failures = [] if data_class not in DATA_CLASSES: failures.append(f"check: data class not one of {', '.join(DATA_CLASSES)}: {data_class}") if data_class == "SECRET": failures.append("check: SECRET may never be submitted to any provider") if data_class not in allowed_classes: failures.append(f"check: this caller may send {', '.join(allowed_classes)}, not {data_class}") for label, relative in (("policy", policy), ("decision", decision)): if not os.path.exists(os.path.join(root, relative)): failures.append(f"check: {label} file missing from the checkout: {relative}") return failures def secret_shapes(text): return [label for label, pattern in SECRET_PATTERNS if pattern.search(text)] def build_record(root, env, provider, purpose, data_class, policy, decision, rule, prompt_source=None, session_id=None, conclusion=None, entity_url=None, outcome="allow"): return { "provider": provider, "purpose": purpose, "data_class": data_class, "source_hashes": source_hashes(root, env, prompt_source), "policy_decision": policy_decision(root, policy, decision, rule, outcome), "time": utc_now(), "result_ref": result_ref(env, session_id, conclusion, entity_url), } def serialise(record): """One JSON line. Refuses a record whose field set is not the seven, or that looks like a secret.""" if tuple(record) != FIELDS: raise ValueError(f"record fields must be exactly {FIELDS}, got {tuple(record)}") line = json.dumps(record, sort_keys=True, separators=(",", ":")) shapes = secret_shapes(line) if shapes: raise ValueError("record refused, it contains a value shaped like a " + " and a ".join(shapes)) return line def render(record): rows = ["| Field | Value |", "|---|---|"] for field in FIELDS: value = record[field] if isinstance(value, list): text = "
".join(value) elif isinstance(value, dict): text = "
".join(f"{key}: {item}" for key, item in value.items()) else: text = str(value) rows.append(f"| `{field}` | {text} |") return "### External submission record\n\n" + "\n".join(rows) + "\n" def parse_args(argv): parser = argparse.ArgumentParser(description=__doc__.splitlines()[0]) parser.add_argument("mode", choices=("check", "write")) parser.add_argument("--provider", required=True) parser.add_argument("--purpose", required=True) parser.add_argument("--data-class", required=True) parser.add_argument("--allowed-classes", default="PUBLIC,INTERNAL") parser.add_argument("--policy", default="docs/policies/egress.md") parser.add_argument("--decision", required=True) parser.add_argument("--rule", required=True) parser.add_argument("--prompt-source", default=None) parser.add_argument("--session-id", default=None) parser.add_argument("--conclusion", default=None) parser.add_argument("--entity-url", default=None) parser.add_argument("--out", default=None) parser.add_argument("--summary", default=None) return parser.parse_args(argv) def main(argv=None, env=None, root=ROOT): args = parse_args(argv if argv is not None else sys.argv[1:]) allowed = tuple(name.strip() for name in args.allowed_classes.split(",") if name.strip()) failures = check_preconditions(root, args.policy, args.decision, args.data_class, allowed) if args.mode == "check": for failure in failures: print(failure) if failures: return 1 print(f"check: {args.provider} may receive {args.data_class} under {args.decision}") return 0 # In write mode the submission has already happened, so a failed precondition is recorded # as a refused decision and reported, never turned into a missing line. record = build_record( root, read_env(env if env is not None else os.environ), args.provider, args.purpose, args.data_class, args.policy, args.decision, args.rule, args.prompt_source, args.session_id, args.conclusion, args.entity_url, outcome="allow" if not failures else "refused", ) try: line = serialise(record) except ValueError as err: print(f"write: {err}") return 1 if args.out: with open(args.out, "a", encoding="utf-8") as handle: handle.write(line + "\n") if args.summary: with open(args.summary, "a", encoding="utf-8") as handle: handle.write(render(record)) print(line) for failure in failures: print(failure) return 1 if failures else 0 if __name__ == "__main__": sys.exit(main()) ``` The test, `tests/test_egress_record.py` (134 lines), mirrors the style of `tests/test_ci_checks.py`: a `tempfile` root, a real `git init` and one commit so `git_tree` has something to hash, and `sys.path.insert` plus `from tools.egress import record`. Its nine cases are: the record carries exactly the seven spec fields; source hashes name the tree, the commit and the event payload; no secret in the environment can reach the record (environment polluted with `sk-ant-oat01-...`, `sk-ant-api03-...` and `ghp_...`); a secret-shaped value is refused and nothing is written; check fails when the decision record is not in the checkout; check refuses a class this caller may not send; SECRET is refused even when the caller allows it; write appends one JSON line and a summary table with the expected run URL and session id; write records a refused decision rather than no line at all. A real line it produced in the test run: ``` {"data_class":"INTERNAL","policy_decision":{"decision":"docs/decisions/2026-09-03-egress-policy.md","decision_sha256":"d2901b12...","outcome":"allow","policy":"docs/policies/egress.md","policy_sha256":"c6c18b15...","rule":"claude-review-anthropic"},"provider":"anthropic","purpose":"pull request review","result_ref":{"conclusion":"success","job":"review","provider_session_id":"s-1","run_url":"https://github.com/owner/repo/actions/runs/42/attempts/1","workflow_ref":""},"source_hashes":["checkout-tree:sha1:49e4527b...","checkout-commit:sha1:aaaa...","event-payload:sha256:8d705b91..."],"time":"2026-09-03T10:49:26Z"} ``` Workflow steps for `claude-review.yml`. Add `id: claude` to the existing action step and insert these three: ```yaml - name: Egress precondition (spec section 5) if: env.HAS_TOKEN == 'true' run: | python3 tools/egress/record.py check \ --provider anthropic \ --purpose "review a pull request against CLAUDE.md, the spec and ROADMAP.md" \ --data-class INTERNAL \ --allowed-classes PUBLIC,INTERNAL \ --policy docs/policies/egress.md \ --decision "$EGRESS_DECISION" \ --rule claude-review-anthropic env: EGRESS_DECISION: docs/decisions/2026-09-XX-egress-policy.md # ... the existing anthropics/claude-code-action step, now with `id: claude` ... - name: Egress record (spec section 5) if: always() && env.HAS_TOKEN == 'true' run: | python3 tools/egress/record.py write \ --provider anthropic \ --purpose "review a pull request against CLAUDE.md, the spec and ROADMAP.md" \ --data-class INTERNAL \ --allowed-classes PUBLIC,INTERNAL \ --policy docs/policies/egress.md \ --decision "$EGRESS_DECISION" \ --rule claude-review-anthropic \ --prompt-source .github/workflows/claude-review.yml \ --session-id "$CLAUDE_SESSION_ID" \ --conclusion "$CLAUDE_CONCLUSION" \ --entity-url "$ENTITY_URL" \ --out "$RUNNER_TEMP/egress.jsonl" \ --summary "$GITHUB_STEP_SUMMARY" env: EGRESS_DECISION: docs/decisions/2026-09-XX-egress-policy.md CLAUDE_SESSION_ID: ${{ steps.claude.outputs.session_id }} CLAUDE_CONCLUSION: ${{ steps.claude.conclusion }} ENTITY_URL: ${{ github.event.pull_request.html_url }} - Five details behind those steps. 1. Every action output is passed through `env:` and referenced as a shell variable, never interpolated directly into `run:`. `session_id` is a value the action produces, and `${{ }}` inside a `run:` block is textual substitution, which is a script-injection surface. 2. It needs a row in that page's provenance table and in the admission register. findings.question: What should the recurring review look like, so the ledger is read rather than merely written, and what does it tie to that already exists?
findings.answer:
Three ties, each to something already in the repository, in increasing order of how much human attention they cost.

1. Machine read, on every pull request, through the `checks` workflow that already runs `python tools/ci/checks.py` (`.github/workflows/ci.yml:26`). Add a `check_egress_ledger()` to that file: every line of `docs/runs/egress/index.jsonl` parses as JSON, carries exactly the seven fields, names a `policy_decision.decision` file that exists in the tree, and carries `policy_decision.outcome` of `allow`. Any `refused` line, or any line naming a policy hash that is neither the current `docs/policies/egress.md` nor a hash listed in that policy's history table, fails the build. This costs nothing per run and makes the ledger unignorable: a bad line breaks a required check.

2. Reconciliation, as a run record, on a fixed cadence shorter than the artifact retention window. The roll-up is a normal session task producing `docs/runs/<date>-egress-rollup/README.md` in the format `docs/runs/2026-09-02-roadmap-revision-2/README.md` already establishes: a status first line, a table of what ran, and a statement of what was kept where. Its work is: list every run of `claude-review` and `claude` from the Actions API, download each run's `egress-*` artifact, append the lines to `docs/runs/egress/index.jsonl`, and report any run of those two workflows whose conclusion is not `skipped` and that has no ledger line. That last comparison is the completeness test; without it the ledger only proves that the runs which recorded, recorded. The roll-up lands as a draft pull request into `main` and the owner merges it, which is the repository's only write path anyway.

3. Gate read, at each phase boundary, extending a criterion that already exists. The operating model's Phase 2 exit already says "P2-2 `egress.jsonl` across the phase lists only `PUBLIC` with zero violations and matches transcript tool-use events" (line 857). Decision 12 should add the Phase 0 and Phase 1 form of that same criterion: across the phase, every line names Anthropic as provider under the recorded decision, every line's class is at or below the class the policy permits for that workflow, zero lines carry `outcome: refused`, and the run count from the Actions API equals the ledger line count. Tying it to the existing exit-criteria mechanism means the ledger is read by whoever closes a phase, not only by whoever is curious.

One thing the review should not be: the `claude-review` workflow itself reading the ledger. That is circular, since a run reviewing its own egress record is another egress, and its finding would not be an authoritative result under CLAUDE.md's authority rule in any case.

findings.question: What residual gap does the mechanism not close, so the decision record can name it honestly?
findings.answer:
Eight, in the order a reviewer should care about them.

1. The ledger records availability, not readership. `checkout-tree` bounds what was on disk; the model chooses what to read, and that choice is not observable from inside the run. The only artifact that would show it is `execution_file`, which is the full transcript in `RUNNER_TEMP` and which the action's own input documentation says may contain secrets, so it is neither retained nor hashed. Every line of the ledger is an upper bound.

2. The bound is not even tight for `claude.yml`. Tag mode fetches issue and pull request comments and reviews through the GitHub API during the run, after `GITHUB_EVENT_PATH` was written, and the workflow grants `contents: write` and an API token. Text created after the event payload was written can be submitted and is covered by no hash in the record.

3. The recorder lives inside the thing it records. A pull request that deletes the two record steps still triggers `claude-review`, because `pull_request` runs the workflow file from the pull request head. The `checks` job would fail that pull request, but the egress would already have happened. `issue_comment` is safer: GitHub only runs the workflow file from the default branch, so branch protection on `main` covers `claude.yml`. There is no in-repository fix for the `pull_request` case; only the owner reviewing the diff before merge covers it.

4. Data class is a declaration. `INTERNAL` is a literal in the workflow. Nothing verifies that the tree at that commit holds no `PROJECT_CONFIDENTIAL` bytes, and no script can, because classification is a judgment about content. If bid drawings or evidence crops ever enter the repository, the ledger will keep saying `INTERNAL` and will be wrong.

5. One record per run, one timestamp. A 30 or 60 minute run makes many API calls; the record marks the window's end, not each call. There is no per-call ledger and building one would mean parsing the transcript, which point 1 rules out.

6. Retention and roll-up. Artifacts and logs default to 90 days. Until the record is rolled up into a commit, the ledger is transient. A run whose artifact expires before a roll-up is unrecoverable, and the roll-up is a human obligation with no mechanical trigger in the repository today.

7. Cancellation and runner loss. `if: always()` covers a failed action step, but a runner that dies, a hard job cancel, or a cancellation by `concurrency` may end the job with the submission made and no record written. The reconciliation of finding 4 is what turns that into a visible gap rather than a silent one, and only if run metadata outlives the run.

8. The record says nothing about what happens at the provider. Retention, training use, subprocessors and deletion at Anthropic are governed by whichever commercial or consumer terms the token belongs to, not by anything this repository can measure. Decision 12 should state which terms apply and cite them; the seven-field record is evidence that a submission was made under a named decision, not evidence about the recipient's handling.

findings.question: What should the structure of docs/policies/egress.md be, and what must each section state?
findings.answer:
Skeleton only. The substance of every rule is the owner's to decide in Decision 12; what follows is the shape and the propositions each section must assert so that no class, session kind, workflow or field is left unstated.

**Title and header block.** Owner, status, the decision record that authorizes it with its date, and the sentence that this policy is what `tools/egress/record.py` hashes into every submission record. A version and effective date, because records hash this file and old records must remain verifiable.

**1. Purpose and authority.** That this file is task P0.9 and implements spec section 5. That it binds every session, workflow, connector and worker in the repository. That where it and `CLAUDE.md` differ, the stricter reading applies until the owner reconciles them. That nothing here authorizes a provider not named in section 4.

**2. The four data classes.** A table with one row per class, and for each: the definition, examples drawn from this repository rather than from the spec's construction examples, the default external rule, and who may reclassify. It must state all four including `SECRET`, and it must state that `SECRET` is never submitted anywhere, never appears in a record, and that a token-shaped value in a record is a failure of the record, not a redaction task. It must say what class ordinary repository content is, since that is the class the two Claude workflows send, and it must say what makes something `PROJECT_CONFIDENTIAL` in a repository that holds no bid data yet.

**3. Session kinds and what each may see.** A table of the environments that exist: local Claude Code CLI, Claude Code web or remote session, GitHub Actions runner, the research browser profile of Phase 2, and any future connector. For each: the maximum class it may hold, the maximum class it may transmit, and the mechanism that enforces it. It must state that a web or remote session never receives `PROJECT_CONFIDENTIAL` bytes, and it must state that a GitHub Actions runner holds whatever the repository holds, so the runner's ceiling is the repository's class, not a lower one.

**4. Approved providers and the workflows that may call them.** A table with columns provider, calling workflow or session, purpose, maximum class, decision record, rule id. The rule id is the string the workflow passes as `--rule`, so the ledger joins to this table. Rows to fill at minimum: Anthropic via `claude-review`, Anthropic via `claude`, and the Phase 0 and Phase 1 uses of Context7 and the GitHub connector that `ROADMAP.md` line 125 records as an exemption. It must also say what is not approved, including that council-style multi-provider routing is off (Decision 12's recommended answer), and it must state the default: any provider not in this table may not be called.

**5. The seven-field submission record.** A table of the seven field names exactly as the operating model declares them at line 733, each with what it must contain, whether it is measured or declared, and what it deliberately does not claim. It must state the labelled forms of `source_hashes` and the sentence that they bound what was made available rather than enumerate what was read. It must name where records are written, in what order of durability, and the roll-up cadence with its relation to the artifact retention setting. It must state that no pull request text, issue text, comment text or model output is copied into a record.

**6. Preconditions and refusals.** The list of conditions under which a submission must not happen, each with the mechanism that stops it: no decision record in the checkout, a class above what the caller may send, `SECRET` in any form, a secret-shaped value in the record, a provider absent from section 4. It must state that these fail closed, meaning the job stops before the call rather than proceeding and logging.

**7. Recording, review and reconciliation.** The three ties of the review design: the `checks` job's ledger check, the reconciliation run record and its cadence, and the phase-exit criterion. It must state who does each and how a discrepancy is reported.

**8. Violations.** What counts as one, following the operating model's rule that any external call absent from the record or from this policy is a `POLICY_VIOLATION`. What must happen when one is found: the record, the escalation, and the fact that a violation satisfies no gate.

**9. Change control and hash history.** That this file changes only through a reviewed pull request; that each version's SHA-256 is listed with its effective dates, so a record hashing an older version can still be checked against the rules that were in force; that a change to the class rules or the provider table needs a new decision record, not an edit here.

**10. Known limits.** The residual gaps of finding 5, stated in the policy itself rather than only in the decision, so that a reader of the policy is not misled about what the record proves. It must say plainly that the ledger records an upper bound of what was made available and cannot show what was read.

One mechanical warning for whoever writes it: `tools/ci/checks.py` fails on any relative markdown link whose target does not exist, and on any em or en dash in `docs/policies`. So the policy must not link to a Decision 12 file before that file is committed, and the two must land in the same pull request or the link must wait.

findings.question: Does adding the mechanism require amending documents that already describe the repository's egress posture?
findings.answer:
Yes, three, and the decision record should say so or the repository will contradict itself the day the secret is added.

1. `docs/roadmap/dynamic-workflow-operating-model.md` section 8, line 725, lists `pr-review` and the other repository workflows with "External providers: none" and "Network in acceptance: deny". Those rows describe Workflow-tool runs, not GitHub Actions, but a reader will take them as the repository's whole egress table. The table needs a row for the two GitHub Actions workflows naming Anthropic as the provider, or an explicit sentence that it covers only Workflow-tool runs.

2. `docs/policies/github-automation.md` section "Egress, and why the secret waits" (lines 33 to 37) states the current position, that the secret waits for a Decision 12 record which "must name Anthropic as an approved provider for this repository's content class and say how each run's submission is recorded". That paragraph is satisfied by this mechanism and should be rewritten to point at `docs/policies/egress.md` and the record steps rather than at a pending decision. Its provenance table also needs the `actions/upload-artifact` row if that step is adopted.

3. `CLAUDE.md` forbids sending `INTERNAL` or `PROJECT_CONFIDENTIAL` material to any external service without qualification. Decision 12 plus `docs/policies/egress.md` is the policy that permits the `INTERNAL` case for two named workflows, so the `CLAUDE.md` sentence needs the exception written into it, or it will read as forbidding what the repository then does every pull request.

One more fact worth putting in the decision, because it narrows the blast radius: Dependabot already opens weekly pull requests against this repository (`.github/dependabot.yml`), and GitHub's own troubleshooting guidance for Dependabot with Actions says secrets for those runs must live in Dependabot secrets "rather than as GitHub Actions secrets". So a Dependabot pull request should evaluate `secrets.CLAUDE_CODE_OAUTH_TOKEN` as empty, `HAS_TOKEN` as false, and `claude-review` should skip without egressing. That is a useful property to state and then confirm on the first Dependabot pull request after the secret is added, rather than to assume.

recommendations.recommendation:
Decision 12 should approve Anthropic as an external provider for INTERNAL-class repository content only, name the two workflows explicitly, and set the class ceiling as a standing condition rather than a one-time judgement.

What actually leaves the repository is narrower than the current policy page says and wider in one respect. The page at docs/policies/github-automation.md line 35 states the workflows send "the pull request diff, CLAUDE.md, ROADMAP.md, and the spec." That is right about the likely content and wrong about the mechanism. Neither workflow pushes files. claude-review.yml runs in agent mode and its first request to Anthropic contains only the prompt text written in the workflow file. claude.yml runs in tag mode and its first request adds pull request or issue metadata, the body, up to 100 comment bodies, up to 100 review bodies with their inline comments, and a changed-file list of paths, change types and counts. Neither mode prefetches file bytes or patch text. Everything else reaches Anthropic because the model asked for it with a tool, and every tool result is then carried in the next request. The reachable set is the whole checkout, about 1.43 MB across 49 files today, plus full git history in the review workflow because it checks out with fetch-depth 0.

Volume is not bounded by anything the repository controls. The action has no max_turns input, neither workflow passes --max-turns through claude_args, and the loop runs until the model stops. The only ceilings are the job timeouts, 30 minutes and 60 minutes, and the tool allowlists. If the decision wants a bounded submission it has to add --max-turns to claude_args in both workflows.

Only one non-GitHub destination receives repository content: api.anthropic.com. The runner also reaches claude.ai to install the CLI on every run, and Claude Code's documented operational telemetry hosts at Datadog unless CLAUDE_CODE_DISABLE_NONESSENTIAL_TRAFFIC is set. The GitHub MCP container at ghcr.io is not pulled, because neither workflow allows an mcp__github__ tool.

Three conditions belong in the record.

First, a class ceiling with a trigger. The approval covers INTERNAL content. When Phase 3 or Phase 4 puts anything the section 5 table calls PROJECT_CONFIDENTIAL into a path the checkout contains, the approval lapses and needs the project- and provider-specific approval that class requires. The action reads whatever is in the workspace, with no path filter and no data-class awareness, and .gitignore excludes nothing project related, so nothing structural stops the widening. A checks-job test that fails when a designated confidential path becomes readable at the reviewed commit would turn the ceiling into something enforced rather than remembered.

Second, the seven-field record. The action emits none of the seven fields on its own. Provider, purpose and time are derivable from the workflow run. The result reference can be the run URL plus the session_id output. The policy decision is the Decision 12 record itself. Source hashes are the gap: the action hashes only PR-changed files, and only in tag mode, and it never enumerates what the model read. The one artifact that would close the gap is the execution file the action already writes and exposes as the execution_file output, which contains every message and tool result. Neither workflow uploads it, so today it dies with the runner. Uploading it as a run artifact, or reducing it to a list of paths read with their blob hashes, is what makes the source-hashes field answerable rather than estimated.

Third, one mitigation before the secret is added. Because allowed_non_write_users is empty, the action rewrites the origin remote to embed a live GitHub token in cleartext in .git/config inside the checkout, and file reading is available to the model by default. Nothing in the action redacts tool output; its only redaction covers GitHub token patterns in comment and body text. Adding --disallowedTools with a rule that blocks reads under .git, or accepting the risk explicitly in the record, is a cheaper answer than discovering it after the fact.

Separately, and outside this decision, the Bash permission entries in claude-review.yml line 35 use the form Bash(git diff *) rather than the documented prefix form Bash(git diff:*). If that form does not match, git diff and git log are denied at runtime and the review runs on file reads alone. Worth confirming on the first live run.

recommendations.recommendation:
Use ANTHROPIC_API_KEY from a Console organization under the Commercial Terms. Do not add CLAUDE_CODE_OAUTH_TOKEN. Change the `claude_code_oauth_token` input to `anthropic_api_key` in both `.github/workflows/claude-review.yml` (line 29) and `.github/workflows/claude.yml` (line 44), which is the one-line change `docs/policies/github-automation.md` line 21 already describes.

Four parts of that recommendation rest on published terms quoted above.

| Reason | Published basis |
|---|---|
| Training is prohibited rather than toggled | Commercial Terms section B: "Anthropic may not train models on Customer Content from Services." The Consumer Terms instead say Materials may be used "including training our models, unless you opt out of training through your account settings". |
| Repository content is treated as confidential | Commercial Terms E.1: "Customer Content is Customer's Confidential Information", with the need-to-know limit in E.2. The Consumer Terms page does not contain the word "confidential" at all. |
| Retention is 30 days rather than up to 5 years | Commercial retention article: "we automatically delete inputs and outputs on our backend within 30 days of receipt or generation". Consumer retention is "5-year retention period" when the model improvement setting is on. |
| A processor agreement and sub-processor rights exist | Commercial Terms section C incorporates the DPA; DPA C.1 and C.3 give sub-processor authorization, notice, and a fifteen day objection window. No DPA applies to a subscription. |

The rest is judgement, and should be labelled as such in the decision record.

The governance argument is stronger than the retention argument. On the OAuth path the repository's egress posture is a property of one person's personal account setting, changeable at any time at claude.ai/settings/data-privacy-controls, with no signal inside the repository and nothing to cite in a run record. A repository whose stated purpose is that cited evidence determines truth cannot rest a data class decision on an unobservable toggle. The API key makes the same question an owner-controlled organization property. That is judgement about this repository's governance model, not a statement about Anthropic.

Neither credential is sufficient for PROJECT_CONFIDENTIAL bid drawings. Both workflows send the full pull request diff plus `CLAUDE.md`, `ROADMAP.md`, and the spec, so the class of what leaves is decided by what sits in the repository, not by which secret is used. The strongest published commitments on the commercial path are confidentiality plus deletion within 30 days, with up to 2 years for content flagged by automated systems and up to 7 years for classification scores. My judgement is that Decision 12 should approve Anthropic as an external provider for content at or below `INTERNAL` only, and should state separately that bid drawings, specifications, addenda, quotes, and evidence crops never enter this repository or any branch these workflows read. If that separation later becomes impractical, the next step is a zero data retention arrangement, which is reachable only from the commercial path and only "subject to Anthropic's approval", never from a subscription.

Three operational points, part published and part judgement. First, pin the model and avoid Covered Models: the platform docs say conversation content "is not retained by default; the exception is Covered Models, which require 30-day retention", and name Claude Fable 5.1, Claude Mythos 5.1, Claude Fable 5, and Claude Mythos 5. Second, if US-only processing matters, it must be set as a workspace default in the Claude Console, because `action.yml` at the pinned commit c3d45e8e941e1b2ad7b278c57482d9c5bf1f35b3 exposes no inference geography input; whether a workspace default reaches the action's calls is my inference, not a published statement. Third, the seven-field record spec section 5 requires can be produced per run from the workflow run identifier, the commit under review, the model identifier, and the timestamp, but no published Anthropic page promises a customer-visible record of an individual submission, so the record has to be built on the repository side.

One tradeoff worth stating plainly for the owner: the API key bills per token where the subscription does not, so this recommendation trades a metered cost for contractual certainty. I did not verify pricing.

Do not treat the sub-processor question as closed. The list is contractually incorporated by DPA Schedule 4 and published at trust.anthropic.com/subprocessors, but that page renders client side and every retrieval method available to me returned an empty shell. Its contents are unverified in this report and the owner should read it in a browser before recording Decision 12.
